elements.text: Lack of an adequate, prebriefed aircraft separation plan for the air show performance
Reliance on the air boss’s real-time deconfliction directives instead of a prebriefed plan
Reliance on the see-and-avoid strategy for collision avoidance
Loss of separation between the Boeing B-17G and the Bell P-63F airplanes
Diminished ability of the accident pilots to see and avoid the other aircraft due to flight path geometry
Out-the-window view obscuration by aircraft structures
Attention demands associated with the air show performance
Inherent limitations of human performance that make it difficult to see another aircraft
Lack of FAA guidance for air bosses and air show event organizers on developing plans and performing risk assessments for aircraft not part of an approved maneuvers package
Lack of FAA requirements and guidance for recurrent evaluations of air bosses
Lack of FAA requirements and guidance for direct surveillance of air boss performance
No pilot qualification deficiency or airplane malfunction or failure was identified
No evidence that any flight crewmember’s medical condition or use of medications contributed to the accident
Fighter lead pilot was confused by the air boss’s unclear directives
Fighter lead pilot and position 2 fighter pilot mistakenly aligned with the incorrect show line
The circumstances of this accident underscore the inherent limitations of the see-and-avoid concept for collision avoidance
Air boss’s deconfliction strategy was ineffective because flight paths converged

Federal Aviation Administration and International Council of Air Shows Inc. guidance did not adequately address the need to better mitigate collision risks associated with air boss–directed performances involving multiple, dissimilar aircraft
Air boss–directed performance involving multiple, dissimilar aircraft represents an increased workload for both the air boss and the pilots
Air boss bears the cognitive load of having to create the performance sequence in real time and then issue directives
Pilots must anticipate, understand, and comply with the directives while maintaining visual separation from other aircraft
Lack of administrative controls, such as a prebriefed aircraft separation plan with defined lateral, altitude, and timing deconflictions
A documented safety risk assessment for each performance would allow air show event organizers and air bosses to identify hazards and determine and apply effective mitigations
Recurrent evaluations of air bosses as part of the letter of authorization renewal process would provide objective and ongoing assessments of their performance
Standardized phraseology for references to show lines and other safety considerations that avoids the use of ambiguous terms could help prevent confusion
Lack of guidance and required surveillance tasks for Federal Aviation Administration inspectors assigned to air shows related to the direct observation of an air boss’s performance

The Commemorative Air Force’s lack of a strong, clearly defined safety risk assessment plan resulted in air show production decisions that were not systematically developed to determine acceptable levels of risk
Production decisions were susceptible to influences unrelated to safety, including pressures to deviate from the intended limitations on when revenue passenger rides could be conducted
International Council of Air Shows Inc. role did not involve actively monitoring air shows or the performance of air bosses
